publicSources.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens
publicSources.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

publicSources.title: [grug] Ragged EP train step hangs silently on one rack at d6144 hero scale
publicSources.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

publicSources.title: [grug] Diagnose recurring hero timestamp gaps outside the step timer
publicSources.body:
Diagnose the recurring excess of time between W&B history rows over `throughput/duration` on the 535B-A23B hero run. The pattern occurs before and after disabling QuACK programmatic dependent launch (PDL) in #9183. Its cause and end-to-end throughput cost are unresolved.

A September 16 read of consecutive W&B history rows found:

| Measurement | [Control, PDL enabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-mix-996f4891-step108k) | [Trial, PDL disabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-nopdl-step108k) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| History steps | 108000–108981 | 108778–112667 |
| Eligible adjacent intervals | 976 | 3,886 |
| Intervals with excess >1.2 s | 40.37% | 40.84% |
| Median timestamp interval, quiet / slow | 16.963 / 18.369 s | 16.661 / 18.172 s |
| Median training duration, quiet / slow | 16.704 / 16.717 s | 16.387 / 16.417 s |
| Median excess, quiet / slow | 0.236 / 1.584 s | 0.240 / 1.645 s |

Reproduce the measurement:

1. Fetch unsampled history for the linked runs over the listed step ranges, including `_step`, `_timestamp`, `throughput/duration`, `throughput/hook_time`, and `throughput/loading_time`.
2. For adjacent rows whose `_step` values differ by exactly one, compute `interval = timestamp[i] - timestamp[i-1]` and `excess = interval - duration[i]`. Retain `0 < interval < 60` seconds and `duration[i] < 40` seconds to exclude startup and large interruptions.
3. Classify quiet intervals as `excess < 0.8` seconds and slow intervals as `excess > 1.2` seconds. Compute each column's median independently; median excess need not equal the difference of medians.
4. To locate sustained stretches, take a trailing 12-interval median of excess and retain runs above 1.2 seconds lasting more than 20 intervals. The start-to-start spacing on the trial grows from roughly 67–73 toward 75–83 minutes after startup; control stretches recur roughly 32–42 minutes apart excluding the 116-minute spacing that spans its interruption. The period is not fixed at 80 minutes.

In both groups and both runs, median `throughput/hook_time` is about 4.6 ms and `throughput/loading_time` about 25 microseconds. These recorded timers do not explain the roughly 1.6-second excess in slow intervals.

The [trial build’s training loop](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1160) stops the step timer before callbacks, later metric materialization, and checkpoint handling; the next batch load also falls outside it. [Background tracking](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/background.py#L12) prepares payloads on the training thread and performs tracker I/O on a worker thread. Flat step duration therefore does not establish that the extra timestamp gap is harmless, and timestamp gaps alone do not establish GPU idle time.

The [run tracker](https://mtracker.oa.dev/hero-run-535b) currently attributes the recurring gap to the trial build in its summary, while its September 16 03:25 entry reports the same effect in the control. The evidence above does not establish a PDL regression. The trial also changed the PJRT wheel (#9179), so the build comparison does not isolate PDL's effect on cadence.

Done when:

- Independent trainer progress timing establishes how much of the timestamp excess is real time between completed optimizer steps and how much is deferred logging.
- Measurements locate the delay within the full iteration, explain the recurring stretches, and quantify their end-to-end throughput cost against quiet periods.
- A fix, if needed, is validated across multiple slow/quiet cycles using full-iteration timing; moving time outside `throughput/duration` is insufficient.

Related: #9180 tracks checkpoint-associated spikes in measured training duration; whether it shares a cause with this pattern is unknown. #8870 tracks silent hangs, and #8506 tracks hero operations.

comments.body:
🤖

The 0.77 s gap in the [previous comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9205#issuecomment-5894426715) is the gap on watch steps. The mean over all updates is 0.335 s, or 2.2% of the 15.21 s mean iteration. Finelog's `levanter.metrics` records `throughput/iteration_time`, `throughput/duration`, and `throughput/checkpoint_time` only when `step % 10 == 0` ([`_DETAIL_LOG_INTERVAL`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/telemetry.py#L33)). W&B receives them on every step. The Hero's inline watch runs on the same steps as finelog ([`HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/hero_recipe.py#L52)). All 141 finelog samples in the six hours ending 16:29 UTC (steps 176460–177860) are watch steps.

The table uses unsampled W&B history of [`hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k) for the same steps. `duration` times the train step and `iteration_time` times the full loop iteration, so gap = `iteration_time − duration`:

| Steps | Share | Median gap | Mean `checkpoint_time` | Mean `hook_time` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `step % 10 == 0` (watch) | 10.1% | 0.869 s | 0.105 s | 0.005 s |
| `step % 100 == 99` (coordinated GC) | 1.0% | 3.114 s | 0.447 s | 2.464 s |
| All other steps | 88.9% | 0.230 s | 0.051 s | 0.005 s |

The GC row and the 0.335 s mean exclude step 176999. That step also ran the dropless eval, which adds 58 s once every 3000 updates, about 0.02 s per update. `loading_time` stays below 0.1 ms. On GC steps, rank 0 waits about 0.4 s longer at the checkpoint broadcast. That fits GC duration varying across ranks.

The recurring slow stretches described in the issue body do not appear on this run. Over steps 171469–179469 (8,001 updates), the timestamp excess defined in the issue body has median 0.23 s. 1.4% of intervals exceed 1.2 s, against about 40% on September 16. No trailing 12-interval median exceeds 1.2 s. Over the same 7,998 intervals, the mean timestamp excess is 0.336 s and the mean `iteration_time − duration` is 0.335 s. So the excess is time the trainer spends between optimizer steps, and tracker delivery lag does not explain it.

To split the per-step gap by code location, I used the py-spy thread dumps that Iris already takes of every task pod every 10 minutes (finelog `iris.profile`). The current attempt, 2026-09-27 09:23 to 09-29 23:07 UTC, has 371 dump rounds and 254,509 rank samples from 704 ranks. Some dumps omit one or more of a pod's four rank processes. I excluded 2,460 samples taken during startup or without a main thread. I then assigned each remaining main-thread stack to the training-loop line it was on. 2.03% of those samples are outside the `duration` window, with a 95% interval of 1.7–2.5% from a bootstrap over dump rounds. W&B gives 2.31% over steps 171469–179469, evals included. At the 15.23 s mean iteration, and averaged over ranks, the per-step parts outside `duration` are:

- 0.13 s: W&B payload preparation for the router metrics ([`train.py#L1254-L1261`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1254-L1261)).
- 0.10 s: the every-step save-decision `broadcast_one_to_all` ([`checkpoint.py#L626`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L626)), including time spent waiting for slower ranks. Rank 0's `checkpoint_time` averages 0.06 s, so the other ranks wait in the broadcast longer than rank 0 does.
- 0.04 s: watch-stat logging ([`train.py#L1281-L1282`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1281-L1282)), paid on watch steps only.
- Under 0.01 s each: batch loading, drop-metric sums, and the other `tracker.log` calls.

GC and the eval happen too rarely for 10-minute dumps to measure precisely. Their costs come from the W&B timers above: about 0.03 s and 0.02 s per update. With the three per-step parts, the total is about 0.32 s. The W&B mean over steps 171469–179469 is 0.35 s with evals included.

The logging cost is host-side conversion of JAX arrays. [`_convert_value_to_loggable_rec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/wandb.py#L325-L345) calls `.item()` on each scalar, and each call is a separate blocking device-to-host copy. 2,018 of the 2,132 samples in the router-metric bucket are in `WandbTracker.log` on non-primary ranks. Those trackers set `suppress_logging=True`, but `log` runs `_prepare_log` before it checks that flag ([`wandb.py#L177-L180`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/wandb.py#L177-L180)). The comment at [`wandb.py#L561-L563`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/wandb.py#L561-L563) says a suppressed tracker no-ops every call. Rank 0 does the same conversion on the training thread in `BackgroundTracker._defer`, and all ranks then meet at the save-decision broadcast. Skipping the conversion on suppressed ranks alone may not shorten the per-update gap much. Fewer or batched transfers would shorten it on every rank. We have not tested either change.

96.0% of the steady-state samples are inside the `train_step(state, batch)` call ([`train.py#L1235`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44a4188c197a4b5a314e40cc653f150fa9687dcf/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1235)), and 2.0% are in the `int(state.step)` that follows it. Dispatch holds the main thread for almost the whole device step. Moving the logging after the next dispatch would not overlap it with device work. To hide it, the logging would have to become cheaper or run on another thread.

A higher-rate live profile is not needed for this attribution. `iris task profile <task> cpu` runs `py-spy record` at 20 Hz without `--nonblocking`, which stops every thread of the target process for each sample, NCCL proxy threads included. On the Hero that would stall collectives across the job. A single-rack run would reproduce the per-rank logging and GC costs. It would understate the broadcast wait, which depends on the slowest of 704 ranks.

To reproduce the dump classification, pull main-thread stacks server-side in 2-hour windows:

```sql
SELECT source, captured_at,
  regexp_replace(
    regexp_replace(CAST(profile_data AS VARCHAR), 'Thread \d+ \((?:active|idle)\): "[^M"][^"]*"\n(?:    [^\n]*\n)*', '', 'g'),
    'Thread \d+ \((?:active|idle)\): "M[^a][^"]*"\n(?:    [^\n]*\n)*', '', 'g') AS mains
FROM "iris.profile"
WHERE source LIKE '/marin/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k-coord-49fcf35f/grug-train-hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/%'
  AND captured_at >= TIMESTAMP '<start>' AND captured_at < TIMESTAMP '<start + 2h>'
```

Every rank stack contains a `_run_grug_local (…/train.py:<line>)` frame for the loop statement being executed. A stack inside `broadcast_one_to_all` carries the line of the `checkpointer.on_step` call. Lines 1234–1246 fall inside `duration`. Lines 1217–1232 and 1247–1300 fall outside it.

publicSources.title: [grug] Apply pending query bias during checkpoint evaluation
publicSources.body:
Apply a checkpoint's `pending_qb_betas` before Grug MoE evaluation callbacks run. A checkpoint-only evaluation at its stop step currently exposes the model parameters and EMA parameters without that pending update. The next normal training forward and the sampling restore path apply the update first, so evaluation can score a different routing state from the one the checkpoint would use on its next forward.

The observed score effect was small on two Hero checkpoints. It was still enough to make the first fixed-policy Paloma comparison semantically incomplete. The original `a1` results are superseded by corrected `a2` runs.

This issue is separate from the router-precision proposal in #8435. The omission occurs regardless of router dot precision. The measured impact comes from checkpoints produced by 20 steps on one B200 rack, so it does not establish the size of the effect for other checkpoints or long runs.

Requested behavior: apply the pending query-bias update to both the current and EMA model views used by evaluation hooks. Ordinary progress, logging, and checkpoint callbacks should continue to use the stored state without launching eager query-bias work.

An experimental fix and regression test exist on Romain's fork, but they have not been merged:

- Initial fix: [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860)
- Final scoped fix: [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40)
- Evaluation wrapper: [`train.py`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L679-L693) and [eval-hook application](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1188-L1195)
- Regression test for current and EMA model views: [`test_eval_callback_models_apply_pending_query_bias`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py#L361-L387)

Done when checkpoint evaluation applies the pending query-bias state to current and EMA models, the regression passes, and non-evaluation callbacks avoid this extra work.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Observed behavior

The checkpoint stores `pending_qb_betas` separately from `params`. The training step applies those betas as centered router bias before the next forward, then stores newly computed betas for the following step. The evaluation callback model getters expose raw `params` and EMA parameters. A forced end-of-run callback at an already reached stop step can therefore evaluate the router bias embedded in the parameters and omit the pending update.

The problem appeared while comparing two step-126020 continuation checkpoints under current router arithmetic. Both checkpoints came from the same complete step-126000 native state:

`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-126000`

[`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83) is the observed production source identity for that checkpoint. It does not identify the experimental continuation code.

The experiment branch was based on [`1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1f9c387b6c452895ff58573c2b6117c5500303db). The router arithmetic controls used by the experiment were added in [`f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/f9178348f5237cb2cb591024511d4db693a3910c). The corrected evaluation behavior was introduced in [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860) and scoped to evaluation hooks in [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40).

The two continuations used seed 0, the restored data-loader state, and steps 126000 through 126019:

| Checkpoint | Continuation job | W&B | Checkpoint path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current arithmetic | `/romain/hero-router-current-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/current-a1/step-126020` |
| Preferred FP32 accumulation | `/romain/hero-router-pref-cont-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-cont-step126k-01a0c066-a1) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/checkpoints/preferred-fp32-a1/step-126020` |

### Superseded and corrected evaluations

The `a1` jobs used raw callback model state and are superseded:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22020006 | 0.80684924 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-coord-01a0c066-a1` | [superseded run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-step126020-01a0c066-a1) | 2.22091150 | 0.80714315 |

The `a2` jobs applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update before the same fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation:

| Checkpoint | Iris job | W&B | Macro loss | Macro BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22016478 | 0.80683833 |
| Preferred-trained | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2` | [corrected run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) | 2.22088742 | 0.80713451 |

Applying the pending state changed macro loss by `-0.00003528` for the current checkpoint and `-0.00002408` for the preferred-trained checkpoint. The preferred-minus-current macro-loss delta changed from `+0.00071144` to `+0.00072265`. This correction does not change the router investigation's recommendation, but it makes the evaluation represent the complete checkpoint state.

Both corrected jobs completed all 16 tasks without failures or preemptions. Their extracted metrics are at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/fixed-eval-with-pending-qb-a2.json`, SHA-256 `d13af487ee6b7f54644b9dcb5e3d7a37fdcc6e17420b7cf7476652877f8e9182`.

The final investigation report is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/hero-router-training-report.md`, SHA-256 `454aae5894a78c99752cff47301441c9a8d315b30d5d1ddf1410c069bba73f4c`. The review response that prompted and verified the correction is at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-training-router-01a0c066/evidence/goal-review-response.md`, SHA-256 `a5bfff56802f87c14b6be057f4cbd9e6f86d298906071f28cbe77f532217a3d9`.

### Reproduction

Run from the experimental fork at [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40). Set `SOURCE` to either step-126020 checkpoint above. Because `num-steps` equals the restored state step, the optimization loop takes no step and the forced final callback runs Paloma:


publicSources.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
publicSources.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids

Kimi Delta Attention, the local mixer (layers 0, 1, 2, 4 at d512; D = 512, 4 heads × 128).** ```mermaid flowchart TB kx["x"] --> kq["q = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_q))"] & kk["k = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_k))"] & kv["v = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_v))"] kx --> kg["decay g = −5 · σ(exp(A_log) · (x W_a↓ W_a↑ + dt_bias))

MLA + Inkling, the global mixer (layers 3 and 5 at d512).** ```mermaid flowchart TB mx["x"] --> mq["q = x W_q (full rank, 4 × 128)"] mx --> ml["KV latent = RMSNorm(x W_dkv), 512 wide, learnable gain"] --> mk["k = latent W_uk"] & mv["v = latent W_uv"] mx --> rel["Inkling bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]

Inkling bias added before softmax"] fa --> xsa["XSA: subtract each head's component along its own v"] --> mg["× 2σ(x W_gate), per head, zero-init"] --> mo["W_o → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` **3c. LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing (every layer).** ```mermaid flowchart TB ex["x (512)"] --> fused["one fused GEMM:
router · W_latent↓ · shared-expert gate/up"] fused --> rt["router logits (fp32)

10k-bin histogram each step; router bias = −β, not trained"] rt --> cw["combine weights = σ(unbiased logits) of the top 8,
renormalized to sum to 2.5"] fused --> lat["latent = RMSNorm(x W_latent↓), 256 wide"] lat & cw --> ep["384 SwiGLU experts, hidden 256
pooled-wave EP all-to-all over 8 GPUs, capacity 1.15"] ep --> up["W_latent↑ 256 → 512"] fused --> sh["2 shared SwiGLU experts, 512 → 256 → 512
down projections fused into one GEMM"] up & sh --> sum["routed + shared → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` ¹ AttnRes rolls a new block at layer *i* while `i % max(1, L // 8) == 0` and fewer than 8 blocks exist. At d512 and d768 every layer closes a block. At d1024 (12 layers) and d1280 (14 layers) only layers 0–7 do, so layers 8 and up all accumulate into one running partial instead of their own blocks. **Optimizer routing:** - **MuonH:** every attention and MoE matrix, and every GatedNorm (KDA `W_β` at 2× the MuonH LR). - **AdamH:** lm_head. - **Adam:** embedding, router, attention output gate, norm gains, ShortConv kernels, KDA decay parameters, Inkling weights. - **Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR:** the AttnRes queries. ## Baseline: clean KMA Branch [`fasttrack-moe-kma`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-moe-kma) @ `4eba59cafa`. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. Submit (the default priority is interactive): ``` NO_PROXY="*" uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.launch --submit \ --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a --priority interactive \ --run-id --size d512 --recipe kma --num-steps <8-min steps> --version ``` ## Compute - cw-us-east-02a at **interactive** priority. - **At most 10 active runs at once**, probes included. - **Limit runs above d768** to keep the experimentation rate high. d1024 and d1280 runs take hours and hold a slot the whole time, so save them for changes that have already passed gate 1 or that need extra scales because of curve-fitting risk. - Don't save checkpoints (the launcher default). ## For humans Comment with a research direction for the agent, for example "try X", or "combine A and B". The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. Where they differ from this issue, this issue wins; the main difference is the fixed-time objective. - Run 5–10 experiments per batch, and prioritize human comments when picking the next one. - Ask for clarification in the thread if helpful, but never hold a batch waiting for an answer: state your assumption and correct it in the next batch. - Start at d512. When a change beats the current best by more than 0.005, validate it at d768. - Post **one comment per batch** and edit it as runs finish. Start it with 🤖 and include: - the batch goal, and which human comments it addresses; - a table with one row per run: change | branch@commit | W&B link | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ vs current best; - a 1–3 line takeaway and the planned next batch. - **Branches:** prefix with `ladderclimb_v1_`, and link the exact commit each job ran. - **W&B:** project `marin_moe`, with short prefixed run IDs such as `lc1-b03-…` (names over 128 characters fail at init). - Add the `agent-generated` label to any issue or PR you open. - Keep the **Status** table below updated with a concise chronology of improvements. ## Status ### Current best recipe (d512): candidate 9 **Runtime (adopted 2026-09-30, no ML change):** PGLE (`--pgle-runs 5`) and the XLA autotune cache syncing every 30 min ([`b25ed70f4a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b25ed70f4a)). Together they cut step time by ≈ 6%, worth ≈ −0.010 at fixed time by the rule below (row 17). Paired comparisons keep 2817 steps at d512. **At equal steps (2817): 2.9750 / 2.9791** (seeds 0 / 1, 185–187 ms median step), i.e. **k ≈ 2.52× vs clean KMA**. At d768 (widths scaled to hidden, 7325 steps): **2.7153 / 2.7098**, −0.0051 vs candidate 8 with **107% log-k retention**. The rules, following the MFU-gaming guidance: - changes are judged at equal steps; - 8 active experts stay, and the MoE latent stays at 0.5d; - expert/shared widths scale with hidden_dim; - the recipe must fit d1024 on 8×H100 (candidate 8 does, with attention remat). The d768 check of candidate 7 is in [batch 89](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5863894129). It is the clean KMA architecture plus the pieces below, grouped by kind. Launcher flags are in parentheses. *Speed (same math):* - fp32-accumulating embedding-gather backward (always on) - unrolled router top-k - reshape gate/up split - XLA command buffers - synchronized GC - row-sharded bigram table and its Adam state (`embed2_fsdp=true`) *Attention and logits:* - learnable MLA logit scale, init 4 (`qk_mult=4.0`, `learnable_qk_mult=true`) - tanh lm_head soft-cap 10 (`logit_soft_cap=10`); lm_head z-loss kept - MLA partial key offset (`mla_key_offset=true`) - per-head key RMSNorm on the MLA layers (`mla_k_norm=true`) - per-head query RMSNorm on the MLA layers (`mla_q_norm=true`); free under MLA absorption, since queries aren't cached *KDA:* - Gated DeltaNet-2 channel-wise erase and write gates (`kda_erase_gate=true`, `kda_write_gate=true`) *Embeddings and memory:* - gated value embeddings on the MLA layers (`value_embeds=gated`) - no GatedNorm on the embedding or the lm_head input (`embed_gated_norm=false`, `final_gated_norm=false`) - 524k-row hashed bigram table as an AttnRes source, table LR ×10 (`second_embed=true`, `second_embed_bigram=true`, `embed2_rows=524288`, `embed2_lr_mult=10`) - rank-16 per-channel content gate on the bigram source (`bigram_gate=true`, `bigram_gate_rank=16`) *Experts:* - 512 routed experts, top-8, i.e. sparsity 64 (`num_experts=512`) - one shared expert of width 1.5d instead of two of 0.75d (`num_shared_experts=1`, `shared_expert_intermediate_dim=768`) - ungated ReLU² experts at 1.5× width, routed and shared (`moe_ungated_relu2=true`, `moe_ungated_kernel=true`, `shared_ungated_relu2=true`, `intermediate_dim=384`, `shared_expert_intermediate_dim=384`) *Router and MoE combine (candidate 9):* - router Adam LR ×0.5 (`router_lr_mult=0.5`) - sqrt-softplus combine weights (`router_combine=sqrt_softplus_renorm`) - drop-aware combine renorm: renormalize the surviving slots when an assignment is dropped at capacity (`moe_drop_renorm=true`) - MuonH sigmoid-gate init ×2 (`init_std_mult_gates=2`) *Optimizer:* - Adam β1 0.8 (`beta1=0.8`) - MuonEq per-input normalization (`muon_pre_norm=in`) - Bi-Maxwell momentum on MuonH (`muon_bimaxwell=true`) - MuonH LR decay `1 − p^0.7` (`muonh_decay_power=0.7`); 🤖 **Batch 123: semi-orthogonal LatentMoE projections, frozen or updated on the Stiefel manifold** (intake suggestion from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; [`583d97d120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/583d97d120))

**The idea:** `w_latent_down` / `w_latent_up` are small and shared by every expert in a layer, so they may work as information-preserving maps rather than doing computation. If so, keeping them semi-orthogonal should cost nothing. Freezing them (option B) should then be about as good as updating them with an orthogonality-preserving optimizer (option A).

**Implementation:**
- **Init** (`latent_orthogonal_init`): a Haar-random semi-orthogonal matrix, with orthonormal columns for down and orthonormal rows for up. Every singular value is `std · √d`, which gives the same Frobenius norm as the current normal init, so only the spectrum changes.
- **Option B** (`latent_proj_update=frozen`): both projections stay at their init.
- **Option A** (`latent_proj_update=stiefel`): Skewon from [arXiv 2608.06218](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218), Muon on the Stiefel manifold.
  - With Nesterov momentum M (MuonH's 0.95) and normalized weight Xn, take `N = skew(M Xnᵀ)` and step along `B = −msign(N) Xn`. That's the exact closed-form solution of Muon's subproblem restricted to the tangent space.
  - Then retract with `Xn ← polar(Xn + ηB)`, using cubic Newton-Schulz.
  - `‖ηB‖_F = lr · ‖Xn‖_F`: the same relative step as MuonH's hyperball, at the MuonH LR, so there's no new hyperparameter.
  - CPU tests check three things. The singular values stay at the init value to 1e-4 over 300 steps. On `max ⟨T, X⟩` it reaches 99.96% of the optimum `c‖T‖_*`. Tall and wide matrices both work.
- The paper's own experiments are synthetic (solver accuracy and speed), so this is its first test inside a network.

| arm | what it isolates |
|---|---|
| `ortho` | orthogonal init only, still trained by MuonH |
| `orthofrz` | option B: orthogonal init, both projections frozen |
| `skewon` | option A: orthogonal init, updated with Skewon |

**How to read it:**
- If `orthofrz` ≈ `skewon` ≈ baseline, the projections really are just information-preserving maps.
- If `skewon` beats `orthofrz`, rotating the subspace matters but reshaping its spectrum doesn't.
- If both lose to the baseline, the trained projections do more than preserve information. I'll check that directly against their spectra in the gradient-capture diagnostics, which record the weights of layers 0 and 5.

**New finding: every dense step overshoots.**
- For each applied update I measure r = ⟨g_{t+1}, U_t⟩ / ⟨g_t, U_t⟩. On a quadratic, r = 0 means the step landed on the line minimum and r = −1 means it went twice that far.
- Under MuonH, **100% of dense-matrix steps through step 1700 overshoot**. The median r is −0.2 to −0.6 at step 100, meaning steps go 1.2–1.6× past the line optimum. That's the edge-of-stability pattern, and it matches lag-1 gradient autocorrelations of −0.25 to −0.86 at step 100.

- Routed experts sit near 0 throughout. Their per-step gradients are noise-dominated.

**Why OKLS stopped paying on candidate 9, as far as this shows:**
- The inputs to our matrices are dominated by a few directions: effective rank 2–12% for the value, output, KV-latent and shared-down projections at step 2760. So whitening does most of its work boosting weak input directions by orders of magnitude.
- The resulting direction keeps only **14–33% of Muon's stable rank**, and the step overshoots less.
- Muon's flat-spectrum step ignores the input covariance and makes the same progress per step, more cheaply.
- Weight stable rank under OKLS rises for queries and keys (MLA `w_uk` 70 → 106) and falls for output and down-projections (KDA `w_o` 93 → 70). The blog's "higher stable rank" claim holds only for some of our families.

**One correction to my own method.** My first pass also scored each candidate direction (Muon, OKLS, Shampoo, one-sided, SGD) by its first-order gain on the next batches. That's confounded: those gradients come after the run already stepped along roughly the Muon direction. Every gain came out negative, which is how the overshoot showed up. Those scores aren't reported, and the overshoot ratio replaces them.

**What would make OKLS worth another look.** Each item comes from a measurement above:
1. **Output-side-only whitening.** B is well-conditioned, and whitening only that side avoids amplifying near-dead input directions.
2. **A damped input factor** (A + λ·tr(A)/m·I), sweeping λ rather than LR.
3. **Targeting overshoot directly.** Overshoot is uniform across families early on, so a per-matrix step cap during the first third of training is a cheaper test than any preconditioner.

🤖 **Batch 132: two new ideas from a literature scan** (d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; runs from now on carry the adopted PGLE)

I had a scout sweep 2025–2026 papers and speedrun records for untried ideas that fit the constraints (top-8, sparsity 64, latent 0.5d, no tokenizer changes). Of the 13 it returned:
- **Already done or already in the model:** XSA (b37/b39), the attention output gate (MLA already has `attn_gate`), asymmetric logit soft-cap (b32), global-batch load balancing (our QB counts are already `psum`-ed over the whole batch), and a separate V query in AttnRes (batch 129, closed).
- **New and cheap enough to run now:**

| arm | idea | source |
|---|---|---|
| `kdaneg` | negative-eigenvalue KDA: the delta coefficient β ∈ [0, 2] instead of [0, 1] (an existing but never-reported `kda_beta_negative` flag) | Grazzi et al., ICLR 2025 ([arXiv 2411.12537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12537)); Complex KDA ([arXiv 2609.24797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24797)) |
| `hero` | **HERO-MoE router history** ([`4b07c54fac`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4b07c54fac)): each router adds `(ρ·H) W_R` to its logits | [arXiv 2609.32581](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.32581) |

**HERO-MoE details:**
- `H` holds the earlier layers' detached router softmax distributions, and `W_R` is learned: `[L, (L−1)·E, E]`, Adam-trained, uniform init at ±1/√(d + (L−1)E).
- `ρ` RMS-matches `H` and scales it by √(n_prev / (L−1)), as in the paper.
- The bias goes through the router's existing seed-bias input, so the MoE kernels don't change.
- Tests: with `W_R = 0` the model is identical to candidate 9, and every layer after the first gets a gradient.
- The paper reports −0.021 training loss and 31% lower peak expert load at 8B-A0.5B / 100B tokens, for +3.9% time.

**Later** (they need data-loader and EP-capacity work): batch-size warmup, sequence-length warmup (SkyLadder), and FP8 expert GEMMs.

- So nothing gets dropped or re-scaled before the 1e24 projection; candidate 9 carries to d1024 and d1280 unchanged. d1280 finishes in about 6 hours.

**Batch 132 update: negative-eigenvalue KDA diverges.** With β ∈ [0, 2] (`kda_beta_negative`), both seeds hit a NaN loss early: step 107 (seed 0) and step 76 (seed 1), on every retry. Our KDA with the GDN-2 erase/write gates isn't stable with the delta-rule eigenvalues allowed to go negative. Getting there would need the Complex-KDA paper's kernel-side handling, not a range change. Closed. HERO-MoE is still running.

consider new router designs. such as a very low neuron MLP as a router. 

Every token that routes to an expert all shares a high activation along the router vector. Perhaps there is some way we can leverage this symmetry. like perhaps we should remove the component of the token aligned with the router when we send it. So neurons can focus on the differences between tokens that arrive. It also decouples 'increase router contribution' from 'increase neuron activations at the token'. LatentMoE will complicate this.

🤖 **Plan for your router comment ([5905815824](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5905815824)): two arms, implementing now**

**A. A tiny-MLP router, as a residual on the linear one:** `logits = x W_r + W_b · silu(W_a x)`, with 32 hidden neurons and `W_b` zero-initialized.
- It starts exactly as candidate 9, so the MLP only has to learn what a linear router can't express.
- This differs from the low-rank routers that lost earlier: those *replaced* the linear router with a rank-r bottleneck.

**B. Removing the router-aligned component before the expert sees the token.**
- Every token routed to expert e has a large component along the router column r_e. Removing it lets the expert's neurons spend their capacity on how the arriving tokens differ.
- **Handling the LatentMoE:** the router and the latent projection read the same normed input x, and the expert reads `latent = RMSNorm(x W_down)`. The router direction's image in latent space is `u_e = r_e W_down`. RMS scaling doesn't change direction, so projecting `û_e` out of the latent input removes exactly the router-aligned part.
- **As a weight transform:** that projection equals constraining expert e's up-projection to ignore `û_e`: `W_up,e ← (I − û_e û_eᵀ) W_up,e`. It's applied each forward on the weights (E × 256 × 384 multiply-adds, negligible), so the dispatch and expert kernels don't change.
- **Decoupling:** with a stop-gradient on `û_e`, growing the router's alignment no longer raises that expert's neuron activations for the token, which is the separation you describe. The combine weight still carries the router's contribution to the output.

Both get 2 seeds on candidate 9 at d512 with PGLE, paired against 2.9750 / 2.9791.

🤖 **Batch 132 results: HERO-MoE router history loses clearly; negative-eigenvalue KDA diverges** (d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791)

| arm | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | median step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hero`: residual router logits from earlier layers' detached routing ([`4b07c54fac`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4b07c54fac)) | +0.0119 / +0.0132 | **+0.0126** | 189 ms |
| `kdaneg`: KDA β ∈ [0, 2] | NaN at step 107 / 76 | | |

- **HERO-MoE:** the paper's −0.021 at 8B-A0.5B doesn't transfer to our 6-layer, 512-expert router, which is already heavily tuned (router LR ×0.5, sqrt-softplus combine, drop-aware renorm, gate init ×2). Feeding each router the earlier layers' distributions most likely couples routing across layers in a way that costs specialization. The zero-init check confirmed the plumbing matches candidate 9 exactly, so this is the idea, not a bug. Closed.
- **Negative-eigenvalue KDA:** closed, as noted in the batch 131 comment.

**Running now (batch 133): your two router designs** ([`6edb0cf0f9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/6edb0cf0f9), plan in the comment above):
- `rortho`: router-orthogonal expert reads. Each expert's up-projection is projected off the latent image of its own router column. CPU tests check that each expert's response along its router direction is exactly zero, and that the weight change is rank one.
- `rmlp32`: a residual tiny-MLP router, 32 hidden neurons, zero-init output, so it starts identical to candidate 9.

Both were also checked on a 4-device expert-sharded mesh.

🤖 **Batch 133 results: both router designs cost a little, consistently** (d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791)

| arm | Δ s0 / s1 | mean |
|---|---|---|
| `rortho`: each expert's up-projection projected off its own router direction (latent image, stop-gradient) | +0.0020 / +0.0022 | +0.0021 |
| `rmlp32`: residual 32-neuron MLP router (zero-init output) | +0.0028 / +0.0030 | +0.0029 |

**Router-orthogonal reads:**
- The cost is small but the same on both seeds. So the router-aligned component isn't pure redundancy: how strongly a token aligns with an expert's router is itself a useful input feature for that expert (for example, a confidence or strength signal).
- One depth follow-up is running as `lc1-b134-rortho-lrn` ([`57199a7d9f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/57199a7d9f)). It removes a **learned** per-expert fraction α_e of the direction: `(I − α_e û_e û_eᵀ) W_e`, with α_e zero-initialized, so the model starts at candidate 9 and chooses how much each expert should ignore. If the α's stay near 0, the idea is closed; if some experts pull theirs up, those are worth a look.

**Tiny-MLP router:** a nonlinear residual on the linear router makes routing slightly worse. Together with HERO-MoE (+0.0126) and the earlier low-rank routers, that says the linear router plus candidate 9's combine is hard to beat at this scale. Closed.

🤖 **Candidate 9 at d1280: 2.3967, k ≈ 2.01× vs clean KMA (2.4710). The 4-rung fit projects 1.710 vs 1.727 at 1e24, so gate 2's projection test passes.** ([lc1-b125-d1280-c9-ga4ck](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b125-d1280-c9-ga4ck): 16667 data-matched steps, batch 256 through 4 gradient-accumulation microbatches, production priority with checkpoints; 1 seed)

| rung | candidate 9 | clean KMA | Δ | k vs clean KMA | log-k retention vs d512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 (fixed-time, 2 seeds) | 2.9771 | 3.1341 | −0.157 | 2.52× (Status convention) | 100% |
| d768 (data-matched, 2 seeds) | 2.7249 | 2.8229 | −0.098 | 2.06× | 78% |
| d1024 (1 seed) | 2.5147 | 2.5931 | −0.078 | 1.95× | 72% |
| **d1280** (1 seed) | **2.3967** | 2.4710 | −0.074 | **2.01×** | **75%** |

- **Retention is flat from d768 to d1280** (78% / 72% / 75%). The advantage stabilizes around 2× rather than decaying rung by rung.
- **Power-law fits** (asymptote 1.2, baseline FLOP accounting):
  - candidate 9: `L = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`, residuals ≤ 0.007;
  - clean KMA: `1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`;
  - 535B baseline: `1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)`.
- **Projection:**

  | compute | candidate 9 | clean KMA | k vs clean KMA | k vs 535B baseline |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1e22 | 1.953 | 1.988 | 1.68× | 2.89× |
  | 1e24 | **1.710** | 1.727 | **1.48×** | **2.95×** |

  Candidate 9's slope is a bit shallower than clean KMA's, so the multiplier over clean KMA narrows with compute. Against the 535B baseline it holds at about 2.9×.
- **Caveat:** the d512 point is at its fixed-time step count, 18% more tokens than data-matched. That flattens the fitted slope, so the 1e24 multiplier is probably conservative. A data-matched d512 run (2383 steps, 2 seeds) would remove the bias. I can run it if you want the cleanest projection.

The plot at the top now shows all four rungs with candidate 9's fitted curve, and the Status row has the d1280 numbers and the projection.

📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5910532511)):

> Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.
>
> Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.
>
> But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:
>
> 1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
> 2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting
>
> And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.
>
> The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

<!-- belay-intake:5910532511 -->

🤖 **Batch 135: a separate MuonH step for the query/key projections** (intake suggestion from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; [`ba5d62732e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ba5d62732e))

A new `muonh_qk` group takes KDA `w_q` / `w_k` and MLA `w_q` / `w_uk`, with its own LR multiplier and momentum. `w_dkv` stays with the other matrices: it feeds both keys and values. The first step brackets the two hypotheses in the suggestion:

| arm | change | tests |
|---|---|---|
| `qk05` | q/k MuonH LR ×0.5 | (1) q/k norms are only a partial fix, so q/k still want a gentler step |
| `qk20` | q/k MuonH LR ×2 | (2) q/k norms stabilize enough that q/k can take a bolder step |

- **What the diagnostics already say:** at step 100, the q/k matrices overshoot about as much as every other dense family (median r −0.37 / −0.38 for KDA `w_q` / `w_k`, −0.36 / −0.40 for MLA `w_q` / `w_uk`, vs −0.43 to −0.60 elsewhere). So nothing yet singles them out.
- **Next:** if one direction wins, its momentum (`muonh_qk_momentum`) is the follow-up.
- **Earlier related result:** b20 moved all attention matrices together (×1.5 +0.0028, ×0.67 +0.0038, older base). This isolates q/k.

Lets do a deepdive on how Muon is behaving. Train for half the duration. Then lets take one step and compute the gradient. For each matrix, make a plot showing the singular values of the gradient, and then after applying NS. 

The opinionated part of Muon is choosing to upweight the low singular values. We want to see where this decision is accurate. We can view each singular value as being connected to a direction in the input space which activates it, which produces a direction in the output space. Boosting a singular value means we really care about strengthing that relationship. More in input X produces more in output Y. 

There are two ways to evaluate if that signal is accurate: 
-does the gradient hold up locally when we sample new data. We can measure SNR via mean(behavior)/square(behavior)
-is the gradient useful beyond nonzero step-size (something can accurately estimate the global gradient, but its not stable for a real step-size change in weights)

Taking an actual step may be too computationally heavy. What we can do to estimate 2 is to repeat the process for n steps in the same local neighborhood. If a gradient aligns across those points, it indicates the direction is consistently downhill in that whole neighborhood, and is likely robust to a step-size update.

Think through this carefully before executing, using clean math and awareness of how much compute it will cost.

🤖 **Plan for the Muon deep dive ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5916346431)): the math, the design and the compute, before running it**

**The question.**
- Write a matrix's gradient as `G = U Σ Vᵀ = Σ σ_i u_i v_iᵀ`. Direction i is "more of input v_i produces more of output u_i".
- Muon steps along `−η O` with `O ≈ Σ u_i v_iᵀ`: every direction gets the same weight. SGD would weight direction i by σ_i. Relative to SGD, Muon boosts the small-σ directions.
- **Per-direction payoff:** to first order, the step changes a batch b's loss by `−η Σ_i s_i(b)`, with `s_i(b) = u_iᵀ G_b v_i`. So `s_i(b) > 0` means direction i of Muon's step lowers batch b's loss. Boosting direction i pays exactly when `s_i` is reliably positive on data and positions the step will actually meet.

**Design:** one probe inside a normal candidate 9 run at d512, at half duration (step 1408).

- **Matrices:** the 46 captured by the batch 120 gradient capture, covering every family (KDA and MLA projections, shared expert, LatentMoE projections, router, 4 routed experts each in layers 0 and 5).

1. **Basis and spectra.** At θ₀, average the gradient over 8 batches (set A): `G_A = U Σ Vᵀ`. For each matrix, plot σ_i of `G_A` and the singular values after Muon's own Newton-Schulz (quintic, 5 steps).
   - That shows how much each direction is actually boosted: NS gives ≈ 0.7–1.2, not exactly 1.
   - The basis is fixed from set A. It is never scored on its own batches, since there `s_i = σ_i > 0` by construction.
2. **Does it hold up on new data?**
   - **Measure:** on 64 held-out batches (set B), compute `s_i(b)` for every direction.
   - **Report:** the consistency `c_i = mean_b s_i / RMS_b s_i` (1 = the same helpful sign and size on every batch, 0 = pure noise, negative = the reference batch was misleading), against σ-rank.
   - **Also report** `E[s_i]` itself, the expected per-direction payoff.
   - **Muon vs SGD:** compare how well Muon's flat weighting and SGD's σ-weighting line up with that payoff profile, as cosines against `E[s]`.
3. **Does it hold over a real step?** This is your neighborhood test.
   - **Measure:** the run keeps training normally for 32 steps. At each point θ_k on that trajectory, compute `s_i(θ_k)` on a **fixed** set of 4 evaluation batches, with the same θ₀ basis.
   - Fixing the data removes data noise, so the only change is from the parameters moving. And the neighborhood is exactly where training goes.
   - **Report:** the across-position consistency `c_i^pos = mean_k s_i / RMS_k s_i`, and how many steps each direction's sign survives, binned by σ-rank.
   - If a small-σ direction flips sign within a step or two, its boost is consumed or overshot by the step itself. That would tie back to the edge-of-stability overshoot measured in the OKLS deep dive.

**Compute.**
- 8 + 64 + 32 × 4 ≈ **200 extra forward/backward passes**, about 1 train step each (≈ 0.19 s), so **≈ 40 s of GPU time** plus one compile.
- The SVDs of 46 matrices up to 768 × 512 are negligible on GPU.
- The 32 trajectory steps are the run's own training steps, so training isn't disturbed and the run finishes as a normal candidate 9 run.
- Outputs are about 9 MB: per matrix the spectra, `s_i` for 64 batches, and `s_i` at 33 positions.
- Plots go on the diagnostics artifact next to the OKLS page.

**Caveats:**
- The analysis uses the gradient's SVD. MuonH actually orthogonalizes Nesterov momentum after pre-norm and a hyperball step, so I'll also report the basis from the momentum buffer at θ₀ as a check.
- It is one checkpoint in one run. If it's informative, repeating at step 300 and step 2600 gives the early and late picture for another ~40 s each.
We can consider dropping logit z loss now that we have softcap.

publicSources.title: [iris] Decide whether jobs may require a named NVLink rack
publicSources.body:
## TL;DR

- **Decision:** Should an Iris Kubernetes job be able to require one specific NVLink rack?
- **Need:** `group_by="nvlink.domain"` keeps a gang in one rack but does not choose which rack. A job limited to rack 392 needs to name it.
- **Current gap:** Iris skips that exact-rack constraint when building a Kubernetes Pod and lowercases the case-sensitive rack label before serialization.
- **Proposal:** [Draft PR #9478](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9478) would let a job require `nvlink.domain == "DH1-392-US-EAST-08A"`. The job could not run on another rack if the requested rack is missing or full.
- **Scope:** This feature would not reserve Hero training racks or prevent Batch jobs from using spare nodes there.

A read-only audit on September 26 found three Batch jobs using 24 GPUs on six other nodes in three of Hero's 11 training racks. It found no GPU double-booking and did not measure training harm. No placement with the changed controller has been tested live.

<details>
<summary>Evidence: placement audit, current code, and a local test failure</summary>

**Placement audit.** Iris controller `task_attempts` showed Hero using 16 nodes on each of 11 racks (176 four-GPU tasks). Racks 124, 125, and 129 each had 18 labeled nodes: 16 used by Hero and two by one Batch job. Captured Kubernetes node labels mapped the nodes to racks; FineLog `iris.profile` samples confirmed the Batch tasks ran there. The audit did not compare training speed with and without Batch work. A separate job requested only `group_by="nvlink.domain"`, so its placement did not test an exact-rack request.

**Actual rack label.** The captured Kubernetes node snapshot included `s1mwxs64` with `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain=DH1-392-US-EAST-08A`. The uppercase characters matter for an exact label match.

**Current code.** [Gang topology](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L285-L292) selects the `nvlink.domain` level without a rack value. The [Pod selector mapping](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L179-L183) lists only `pool` and `region`; [unknown keys are skipped](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L335-L346). [String constraints are lowercased](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L106-L110) before they are sent.

**Local reproduction.** Adding only the missing Pod mapping produced this failure for an illustrative uppercase rack label. It shows why the label's case must also survive serialization:

```text
assert manifest["spec"]["nodeSelector"]["ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain"] == rack
E AssertionError: assert 'dh1-001-us-east-08a' == 'DH1-001-US-EAST-08A'
```

The [draft PR's regression test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a30e700ae2cc164e28b8f244a8fe9a65f8584454/lib/iris/tests/cluster/backends/k8s/test_pod_manifest.py#L681-L693) checks that the exact label survives controller storage and reaches the Pod's selector and required affinity.

</details>
